headings: What a moral theory should explain
Fifteen discussion questions from each response
introHeading: Testing the claim to objective morality
intro: The original ten prompts and two response tracks are restored in order. Editorial revisions distinguish logical coherence from practical usefulness, objectivity from context independence, and moral reasons from psychological motivation. The original lists, examples, quizzes and discussion sections remain in their response positions.
description: Examine the foundations, consistency, guidance, accessibility and authority claimed by objective moral systems through the original ten-prompt conversation.
highlights: A coherent claim need not yet be a well-supported or practically complete theory.
Relevant circumstances can change an objective judgment without making it a matter of preference.
A reason to act and a desire to act are different things.

replacements.1.1.0: At minimum, the system must state what it means by objective moral facts and make mutually consistent claims about them. A defensible, usable system faces further demands concerning justification and guidance. These are not all logical conditions on the existence of moral facts. The following eight considerations separate those tasks.
replacements.1.1.1: Ontological Foundation for Morality: Explain what moral facts are and whether they depend on attitudes. A theory may treat some facts as fundamental, but must defend that stopping point; merely naming reason or God does not establish a foundation.
replacements.1.1.2: Universalizability: Apply the same standard where the morally relevant circumstances are the same. Identity, promises and relationships can matter when the theory explains why; an arbitrary exemption cannot be justified merely by calling it objective.
replacements.1.1.5: Internal Consistency: Avoid affirming a claim and its denial in the same respect. Consistency permits a theory to be true; it does not prove its premises or guarantee reliable judgments.
replacements.1.1.9: These eight considerations assess different achievements: coherence, justification, explanation and practical guidance. Failure to settle a dispute may expose incompleteness without establishing contradiction. The later prompts examine each demand rather than assuming that one checklist establishes objective morality.
replacements.1.2.0: A coherent claim to objective moral facts must specify its meaning and avoid contradiction. To justify and use that claim, we should also ask the following seven questions. Their importance does not make each one a logically necessary condition of moral reality.
replacements.1.2.2: Universal applicability: Apply standards consistently to relevantly similar cases. An objective obligation may depend on a promise, a relationship or an agent’s capacities; it need not impose the same action on everyone.
replacements.1.2.7: Motivational force: Explain why the alleged facts give agents reasons, and separately how agents can become motivated by those reasons. An unmoved agent does not, just by being unmoved, disprove a moral claim.
replacements.1.2.8: Passing these checks does not establish truth or agreement. Contradiction undermines coherence; lack of evidence undermines justification; unusable advice undermines practical adequacy. Keeping those failures separate makes criticism more precise.
replacements.2.1.0: Ontology asks what exists and what makes a claim true. Here the question is what could make a moral judgment true independently of people’s endorsement. Objectivity does not itself entail that every obligation is timeless or unaffected by circumstances. The original alternatives below offer different answers, with some overlap.
replacements.2.1.7: Non-natural Moral Properties: On this view moral properties cannot be reduced to natural properties. They need not inhabit a separate Platonic realm; “non-natural” does not mean a lesser degree of abstraction. The theory must explain both their normative role and our grounds for believing in them.
replacements.2.1.9: Moral Emergentism: One proposal is that moral properties arise with complex forms of life and relationship. The emergence of cooperation or moral beliefs alone does not establish objective moral facts. A further argument must explain why the emergent feature gives reasons or obligations, rather than merely describing behavior.
replacements.2.1.11: Kantian Ethics: Kant grounds moral obligation in rational agency and tests maxims through universal law. Later Kantian constructivists develop related accounts of justification through rational procedures. Such accounts should not simply be classified as discoveries of independently existing moral objects: their relation to realism is disputed. See Kant’s Groundwork, especially the preface and second section.
replacements.2.2.0: An ontological account should explain what makes moral claims true. For a robust realist, their truth is not constituted merely by our approval. This is different from saying that moral facts cannot concern mental states: suffering and intentions may be morally relevant even when their relevance is not a matter of anyone’s approval.
replacements.2.2.3: 2) Natural moral realism identifies or grounds moral properties in natural features, such as facts about welfare. A theory must defend that connection; facts about rational agency or consciousness do not yield obligations simply by being facts.
replacements.2.2.5: 4) Objective naturalist views may identify moral properties with natural properties. Merely saying that moral facts supervene on natural facts—that no moral difference occurs without some natural difference—does not establish reduction or explain which moral facts obtain. This option overlaps with item 2.
replacements.2.2.6: 5) Moral non-naturalism treats moral properties as irreducible to natural properties. It overlaps with item 1; the distinction here is that non-naturalism need not posit a separate moral realm.
replacements.2.2.7: Independence from human endorsement is the central realist claim under examination. Theories that construct standards through justified rational procedures require separate assessment; dismissing them as mere projection would assume the disputed conclusion. Each proposal must explain why its claimed basis supports morality.
replacements.3.1.3: Rational Consistency: Equal relevant circumstances should receive equal judgments under the same standard. That blocks one kind of arbitrary exception, but does not establish impartiality or objectivity by itself: an objectionable rule can be applied consistently.
replacements.3.1.12: Universalizability is useful here as a demand for consistency across relevantly similar cases. It does not by itself prove an impartial standard, a complete set of general rules, or objective moral truth. The unresolved work is to justify which similarities and differences matter.
replacements.3.2.0: Universalizability requires care: the same standard should apply when all morally relevant features are the same. It does not require identical acts in different circumstances. A promiser may owe something that a stranger does not, even if the obligation is objective.
replacements.3.2.1: Distinguish independence from approval from independence from circumstances. A duty can depend on what happened, what an agent can do and whom an action affects without becoming true merely because a culture endorses it.
replacements.3.2.3: 1) Scope – Specify which agents and affected beings a principle concerns. A rule for promise-makers need not apply to beings unable to promise. Moral patients—beings whose treatment matters—need not themselves be rational agents.
replacements.3.2.6: 4) Generalizability – General rules help transfer judgments between cases. Whether every sound moral judgment can be captured in a finite, exceptionless rule is a further dispute, not something objectivity alone settles.
replacements.3.2.7: 5) Non-indexicality – “I ought to help here” can express an objective claim once the speaker, place and circumstances are fixed. Context-dependent language is not equivalent to preference-dependent truth.
replacements.3.2.8: 6) Modal Robustness – A claim about what holds in every possible world is stronger than a claim about objective truth here. If capacities or consequences differ, a particular obligation may differ too. Necessity requires its own argument.
replacements.3.2.9: For example, a rescuer who can safely reach a person may have a duty that a distant observer lacks. This is a difference in morally relevant circumstances, not necessarily a difference in standards.
replacements.3.2.10: A defense of objectivity must explain why a standard is warranted independently of endorsement. Consistent application helps test it, but consistency alone is also available to some relativist accounts.
replacements.4.1.0: Logical consistency rules out affirming and denying the same claim in the same respect. Conflicting considerations are not automatically contradictions: a reason to keep a promise can coexist with a stronger reason to prevent harm. The examples below ask whether a theory has contradictory final verdicts, competing reasons, or merely inconsistent application.
replacements.4.1.2: If a system treats both “maximize overall well-being” and “never lie” as exceptionless final requirements, some cases will make them conflict. Utilitarianism concerns total or overall welfare, not simply benefiting the largest number. A pluralist can instead treat considerations as defeasible, provided it explains how a final judgment is reached.
replacements.4.1.8: A theory may change over time without containing a contradiction at a given time. The concern here is whether revisions have reasons or merely track convenience. Revising an earlier error can improve consistency.
replacements.4.2.6: 5) Ethical Abduction – Inferring a principle as the best explanation of judgments is defeasible: later cases may overturn it. Do not mistake it for deductive proof. “If this principle, then this verdict; this verdict; therefore this principle” affirms the consequent and does not establish the principle.
replacements.4.2.7: Consider: A) Minimizing total suffering is the highest imperative. B) Sometimes causing suffering is required. These statements are not necessarily inconsistent: causing a lesser harm might be the only way to prevent a much greater harm.
replacements.4.2.8: A genuine contradiction would be: A) Causing any suffering is always prohibited, without exception. B) Causing suffering in this very case is permissible. Both cannot hold in the same sense under the same conditions.
replacements.5.1.19: Action guidance connects principles with choices, including choices made under uncertainty. A useful system distinguishes required, permitted and prohibited acts and explains unresolved tradeoffs. It need not promise a certain answer to every problem in order to improve deliberation.
replacements.5.2.0: A system offered as a practical guide should connect its moral claims to decisions. This is a demand on its usefulness and application, not a proof that inaccessible moral facts could not exist.
replacements.5.2.2: 1) Decision Procedures – Provide usable reasoning methods and acknowledge their limits. A criterion of rightness states what makes an act right; a decision procedure helps an uncertain agent choose. They need not be identical, and a complete algorithm is not required.
replacements.5.2.3: 2) Resolution of Moral Dilemmas – Explain how competing reasons should be assessed, which options remain permissible and where uncertainty persists. A system need not manufacture a unique answer when its commitments do not supply one.
replacements.5.2.7: For example, an act-utilitarian criterion selects the action with greatest overall welfare. An agent who cannot know all consequences needs a practical method involving evidence, probabilities and comparison of alternatives. The criterion alone is not such a method.
replacements.5.2.8: W. D. Ross instead describes several prima facie duties: genuine moral considerations that can be outweighed. Their relative importance requires judgment in the particular case, not a mechanical ranking. His The Right and the Good, chapter II uses promise-keeping and relief of distress to illustrate this.
replacements.5.2.9: The practical test is whether the theory improves deliberation: identify affected people, relevant facts, competing reasons and what would change the decision. Sometimes guidance consists in narrowing the defensible options or seeking missing information.
replacements.5.2.10: A theory with no usable guidance fails as a decision aid. That failure alone does not disprove objectivity; it shows that the claimed moral facts have not yet been connected adequately to our choices.
replacements.6.1.0: Epistemological accessibility concerns our grounds for knowing or justifiably believing moral claims. Understanding a rule, agreeing with it and being justified in accepting it are different achievements. A useful account explains methods of inquiry and possible error without guaranteeing consensus.
replacements.6.1.8: Definition: Intuitions can supply starting points for inquiry, but familiarity is not evidence of infallibility. A theory should explain both stable judgments and their possible distortion by prejudice or interest. Example: Aversion to unprovoked violence invites examination of harm and justification; it does not settle every contested case.
replacements.6.1.12: Definition: Inquiry should understand cultural context without treating acceptance as justification. Example: A person may value family participation in a decision; that differs from having a choice overridden. The theory must explain whose reasons matter and how coercion is identified, rather than assuming that community custom resolves the issue.
replacements.6.1.15: Accessibility requires an account of understanding, justification and correction. Disagreement can remain after serious inquiry. The important question is how reasons are assessed and improved, not whether a method makes everyone agree.
replacements.6.2.4: 3) Opacity Considerations – Specify what can be known, what can only be estimated and what remains inaccessible. Do not claim both complete inaccessibility and detailed knowledge of the same alleged facts.
replacements.6.2.7: Some non-naturalists appeal to rational intuition or reflective judgment; this need not mean a special sensory organ. Theistic accounts may appeal to revelation, reason or both. In either case, naming a faculty does not establish its reliability: conflicting apparent deliverances require criteria of assessment.
replacements.6.2.10: If no evidence could count for or against a claim, our justification for asserting it would be unclear. That epistemic failure does not logically entail that the alleged fact is nonexistent. Accessibility connects a proposed reality to responsible belief about it.
replacements.7.1.0: Normative strength concerns the reasons a system claims to give us: why ought we comply? Psychological influence concerns whether we actually want to comply. The following eight topics matter, but motivation, emotional resonance and social enforcement must not be mistaken for justification.
replacements.7.1.2: Definition: Authority needs justification, not merely recognition. Example: A democratically enacted law may command public trust while remaining unjust. Procedure and acceptance can matter to legitimacy without proving the moral content correct.
replacements.7.1.4: Definition: Internal motivation helps explain compliance, but a person can recognize a duty and resist it. Example: Environmental concern may motivate conservation; whether a particular action is required still depends on reasons about harm, responsibility and alternatives.
replacements.7.1.6: Definition: Rational persuasion offers reasons that withstand objection. Example: Cooperation may benefit everyone, but moral claims also address cases where helping costs the agent. A justification limited to personal advantage cannot by itself explain duties in those cases.
replacements.7.1.8: Definition: Emotion can make morally relevant suffering vivid without settling what we ought to do. Example: A moving appeal may motivate generosity while directing attention away from less visible but greater needs. Emotional force requires critical assessment.
replacements.7.1.12: Definition: Practical guidance makes reasons usable; it does not create their authority. Example: Clear workplace rules help people act, but the rules still need justification in terms of fair treatment, interests or rights.
replacements.7.1.14: Definition: Reflective equilibrium revises principles and considered judgments in light of each other and relevant arguments. Agreement within the resulting set is a form of coherence, not a guarantee of truth. Example: Judgments about punishment may prompt refinement of a fairness principle, while that principle challenges biased judgments.
replacements.7.1.16: Definition: Social reinforcement can sustain a practice without establishing its moral authority. Example: Hospitality can be encouraged through custom; an exclusionary custom can be reinforced just as effectively. The fact of reinforcement leaves the justification question open.
replacements.7.1.17: A convincing account must distinguish a reason’s authority from the forces that make people respond to it. This preserves the central challenge: why should someone comply even when doing so is unpopular, emotionally difficult or personally costly?
replacements.7.2.0: A theory of objective morality should explain the reasons for compliance and their relation to motivation. Whether recognizing a moral judgment necessarily motivates an agent is disputed; it cannot be made a condition of coherence without argument.
replacements.7.2.2: 1) Source of Normativity – Explain what supports the “ought.” A reason conditional on an optional goal does not alone explain a duty alleged to bind someone who rejects that goal. Invoking value, agency or divine authority leaves this explanatory task to be completed.
replacements.7.2.3: 2) Overriding Force – State whether moral reasons always override competing considerations and defend that claim. Their weight must not be inferred merely from calling them moral.
replacements.7.2.4: 3) Moral Motivation – Explain how agents can respond to reasons, including weakness of will and indifference. A reason can be offered without predicting that every agent will find it compelling.
replacements.7.2.6: 5) Judgment and Motivation – Ask whether sincere moral judgment necessarily brings some motivation, or whether an additional desire or disposition is needed. These are competing accounts; lack of automatic synchronization is not by itself a contradiction.
replacements.7.2.7: Some theories connect obligation to constitutive standards of rational agency. They must explain why an agent is bound by those standards and why a moral failure is a failure of practical reason. Moral wrongdoing cannot simply be equated with deductive contradiction.
replacements.8.1.2: Definition: Explain why people have moral intuitions and whether those intuitions are justified. These are different questions. Example: An aversion to gratuitous violence may reflect empathy and social learning; a moral defense must also explain why the harm counts against the act.
replacements.8.1.10: Definition: Distinguish change from progress by providing a defended standard. Example: A theory may explain abolition as progress because slavery violates freedom and equal standing. The evaluative work is done by those reasons, not by the fact that the change occurred later.
replacements.8.2.2: 1) Intuition Consilience – Explain stable patterns in moral judgments while allowing principled criticism of inherited prejudice. Widespread acceptance is something to explain and assess, not a vote that establishes truth.
replacements.8.2.3: 2) Accounting for Moral Data – Treat considered judgments as revisable evidence within an argument. Explain why some deserve weight and others correction; a theory that validates only its own favored judgments risks circularity.
replacements.8.2.4: 3) Dilemma Resolution – Illuminate hard cases by specifying competing reasons and possible resolutions. Acknowledging justified uncertainty can explain a dilemma better than an unsupported decisive answer.
replacements.8.2.7: Utilitarianism explains many duties by their contribution to welfare. Its treatment of rights is also a pressure point: if violating a right would maximize welfare, an act-utilitarian criterion can permit or require it. Whether that is a strength or a counterexample needs argument.
replacements.8.2.9: Explanatory power helps compare theories but does not establish realism by itself. Anti-realists can also explain moral experience, and non-naturalism can itself be a realist position. The comparison must ask what each account explains, at what cost, and whether it justifies moral judgments or only explains why people make them.
replacements.9.1.4: What term concerns a moral system’s justification of reasons for action, distinguished from its psychological success in motivating people?
replacements.9.1.9: What is the term for an account of how people can acquire justified moral beliefs, without requiring universal agreement?
replacements.9.1.10: Which proposal says moral properties arise from complex forms of life and relationship, while still needing an argument for their objective authority?
replacements.9.2.3:
True or False: Objectivity alone entails that each particular moral obligation is unchanged across every possible world.
a) True
b) False
replacements.9.2.4:
Which pair explicitly contradicts itself?
a) “Causing any suffering is always prohibited” and “Causing suffering in this case is permissible”
b) “Minimize total suffering” and “Sometimes causing lesser suffering prevents greater suffering”
c) Both pairs
d) Neither pair
replacements.9.2.5:
What does action guidance require of a practical moral system?
a) Abstract claims with no connection to decisions
b) Usable methods for deliberation that acknowledge limits
c) A guaranteed algorithm resolving every case
d) Personal opinion polls alone
replacements.9.2.9:
Which can contribute to explanatory power?
a) Explaining and critically assessing common intuitions
b) Accounting for considered judgments and possible error
c) Clarifying dilemmas and remaining uncertainty
d) All of the above
replacements.9.2.11: Answers: 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-b, 6-d, 7-a, 8-b, 9-d, 10-a Questions 3 and 4 distinguish circumstance-sensitive obligations from relativism, and conflicting considerations from contradictions.
replacements.10.1.8: What further argument would moral emergentism need to move from the emergence of cooperation or moral beliefs to objective moral authority?
replacements.10.2.2: How should a theory distinguish universal application to relevantly similar cases from identical duties for every possible agent? What capacities or relationships might matter?
replacements.10.2.6: How can a moral realist explain why agents ought to comply while distinguishing that justification from an explanation of what actually motivates them?
replacements.10.2.10: How should realists and anti-realists account for considered moral judgments while allowing that common sense can be mistaken? Does either position require vindicating most inherited beliefs?
